meta.scope: Venezuela batch 4 — Supranational architecture: US sanctions/OFAC general licenses, licensed oil majors, oil-revenue control mechanisms, residual ALBA/Petrocaribe legacy, and key bilateral commercial relationships (US, China, India, Spain/Repsol, UK/Shell/BP, UAE/Qatar gas). Continues under data-quality caution.

candidates.title: Régimen de sanciones de EE.UU. / OFAC Venezuela sanctions
candidates.description: Comprehensive U.S. sanctions architecture targeting the Venezuelan government, PDVSA, the central bank and designated individuals/entities. Continuously amended by general licenses that carve out authorised oil, gas and related activities.
candidates.notes: Dominant external constraint and enabling framework. The regime remains in force; policy has shifted toward incremental expansion of General License carve-outs rather than comprehensive lifting. Continuously cited as the binding condition for lawful commercial engagement with the oil sector.

candidates.title: OFAC General Licenses (GL 46 / GL 50 and successors)
candidates.description: Series of general licenses authorising named international oil companies and defined activities involving Venezuelan-origin oil, gas, petrochemicals and related investment. Core operational carve-out from the broader sanctions regime.
referenced_by: Chevron, BP, Shell, Eni, Repsol, Maurel & Prom operations
candidates.notes: Operational enabler of the recent production recovery. Named majors are authorised to operate upstream and related activities under evolving license terms; royalty and revenue handling is subject to U.S.-controlled mechanisms.

candidates.title: Chevron — licensed oil operations in Venezuela
candidates.description: Longest-standing U.S. major operating under successive OFAC licenses. Principal early channel for resumed commercial oil flows toward the United States.
candidates.notes: Flagship licensed operator. Continuously cited as the bridge that kept a residual commercial link to the U.S. market during the tighter sanctions period and as a core participant under the broader 2026 general licenses.

candidates.title: Majors licenciados (BP, Shell, Eni, Repsol, Maurel & Prom)
candidates.description: Group of European and other international oil companies authorised under OFAC general licenses to conduct oil and gas operations in Venezuela alongside Chevron.
candidates.notes: Expanded licensed-operator set. Their entry/return under the 2026 general licenses is a central feature of the post-transition commercial reopening of the upstream sector.

candidates.title: Fondo / mecanismo de control de ingresos petroleros (EE.UU.)
candidates.description: U.S.-controlled arrangements for the handling of certain Venezuelan oil-related revenues and royalty flows under the post-2026 sanctions and license architecture.
candidates.notes: Critical revenue-governance node. Independent analysis tracks the share of export value that flows through U.S.-administered mechanisms versus direct government or PDVSA channels; transparency remains limited.

candidates.title: ALBA-TCP y Petrocaribe — residual architecture
candidates.description: Bolivarian Alliance and Petrocaribe energy-cooperation frameworks that structured preferential oil supply and political alignment during the 2000s–2010s. Residual institutional and debt relationships persist.
referenced_by: Caribbean and Central American debt-to-Venezuela discussions
candidates.notes: Legacy supranational node. No longer the dominant commercial framework, but residual claims, political references and institutional memory remain relevant to Venezuela’s regional relationships.

candidates.title: Relación comercial petrolera Venezuela–EE.UU.
candidates.description: Bilateral oil-trade relationship reconstituted under the licensed-operator regime. United States has re-emerged as a major (in some recent months the largest) destination for Venezuelan crude.
candidates.notes: Structural commercial reorientation. Share of exports going to the U.S. has risen sharply relative to the China-dominated pattern of the preceding years.

candidates.title: Relación comercial y de deuda con China
candidates.description: Long-standing oil-for-loans and commercial relationship. China was the dominant export destination through the mid-2020s; volumes and relative weight have declined under the post-transition commercial reorientation.
candidates.notes: Legacy and residual partner. Oil-backed debt and preferential supply arrangements defined a major external relationship for more than a decade; the commercial share has fallen as U.S.-licensed channels expanded.

candidates.title: Relaciones comerciales con India y Turquía
candidates.description: Emerging and re-activated oil-trade relationships. India has reappeared as a significant buyer under eased sanctions conditions; Turkey is a recurring political and commercial interlocutor.
referenced_by: High-level bilateral visit and agreement reporting
candidates.notes: Diversification nodes. India in particular has absorbed material volumes in recent periods as sanctions carve-outs and commercial pragmatism reopened previously constrained channels.

candidates.title: Proyectos de gas (Loran, Cardón IV) — partnerships
candidates.publisher: PDVSA / Shell / BP / Eni / Repsol / partners
candidates.description: Key gas-development projects involving international partners (Shell, BP, Eni, Repsol and others) under the licensed or authorised framework. Includes cross-border fields with Trinidad and Tobago.
candidates.notes: Gas-side international partnership node. Complements the oil-focused licensed-major set and illustrates the broader energy-sector reopening under the current sanctions-and-license architecture.

proposed_edges.basis: General Licenses are the operational carve-outs within the broader OFAC Venezuela sanctions regime.
Chevron’s operations are authorised under successive OFAC general licenses.
BP, Shell, Eni, Repsol and Maurel & Prom operate under the same general-license framework.
Revenue-control mechanisms are an integral part of the post-2026 sanctions and license architecture.
U.S. destination volumes are a direct function of licensed production and commercialisation.
China’s residual and historical offtake is a major component of the export-destination structure.
Loran and Cardón IV projects involve the same set of licensed or authorised international partners.
Petrocaribe was historically structured around preferential Venezuelan oil supply.
